question: The Commission’s answer to E-001437/20261 confirms its awareness of the allegations of labour rights violations at the BYD construction site and notes that the European Labour Authority (ELA) has offered support to the Hungarian authorities. Three concerns remain unaddressed. 1.

First, the Commission references the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) as a relevant instrument. However, following the Omnibus I amendments (Directive (EU) 2025/794), the threshold for net EU turnover has been raised to EUR 1.5 billion for non-EU companies. Can the Commission confirm whether BYD currently falls within the scope of the CSDDD?

Second, the Forced Labour Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/3015) applies to products placed on the EU market. As the alleged violations concern a construction site – not a product – the regulation appears to be inapplicable to this case. Does the Commission share this assessment and does it identify a legal gap?

Third, ELA’s lack of investigative powers, confirmed in the Commission’s reply, illustrates a structural weakness as more non-EU companies establish operations in the EU. Does the Commission intend to propose strengthening ELA’s mandate to enable proactive cross-border labour inspections?
answer: 1. While data availability will improve by the time the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) (1) becomes applicable and enforceable on 26 July 2029, currently available data suggest that the ultimate parent company of the European BYD subsidiaries will fall under the scope of the directive. 2.

The fact that regulation (EU) 2024/3015 (2) is focused on products does not imply that a legal gap exists. The regulation is only one of the instruments at the disposal of the Commission and Member States to combat forced labour and must be understood as complementary to other instruments that can be used to address situations of forced labour in Member States, such as national labour and criminal laws. 3.

The European Labour Authority (ELA) plays a supporting and coordinating role in relation to concerted and joint inspections. It does not replace national labour inspectorates or carry out inspections independently; rather, it helps Member States cooperate in enforcing EU rules on labour mobility and social security coordination.

As part of the already announced Fair Labour Mobility Package, the Commission is currently working on a legislative proposal aimed at strengthening the mandate of ELA, including with regard to cross-border labour inspections. The content and scope of the Commission proposal are currently under preparation.
